sat.title: How This Test Actually Works
sat.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome to SAT Notes, episode one. I'm Lehua. Today we answer the question nobody asks out loud. What even is this test? Derek is here, Coach Pono is here, and Kaden is here with a breakfast burrito.
KADEN: It's a second breakfast. First one was at home.
DEREK: Two breakfasts. Bold.
LEHUA: Okay, Kaden, what do you think the SAT is right now? Be honest.
KADEN: Honestly? A four-hour paper test with a lot of reading and one kid sharpening his pencil the whole time.
DEREK: That was true a long time ago. It is not true now. Let me lay it out.
DEREK: The SAT is digital. You take it on a laptop or tablet in an app called Bluebook. It has two sections. Reading and Writing comes first, then Math.
DEREK: Each section is split into two modules. A Reading and Writing module is twenty-seven questions in thirty-two minutes. A Math module is twenty-two questions in thirty-five minutes. So the whole test is two hours and fourteen minutes of testing, with one ten-minute break between the two sections.
KADEN: Wait, that's it? That's like one long movie with all the trailers.
LEHUA: About that, yeah. Way shorter than the old paper test. And most people don't know that.
PONO: Okay, now the part that makes everybody nervous. The test is adaptive. Listen, dis one is important.
PONO: Module one is a mix of easy, medium, and hard questions. Everybody gets a module like that. How you do on module one decides your module two. Do well, and module two is the harder version. Do less well, and module two is the easier version.
KADEN: So if I get the hard one, that means I'm doing bad?
PONO: The opposite. The harder module two is the one that can give you the higher score. If module two feels tough, that is usually good news.
PONO: It's like a rodeo draw. Ride your first horse clean, and they give you the horse that scores big points. The rough horse is the prize.
KADEN: I don't want the rough horse.
PONO: You want the rough horse. Trust me.
LEHUA: And this is why we keep saying module one matters. Each module has its own clock, so rushing module one doesn't save you any time for later. It just costs you accuracy.
DEREK: One more detail. A few questions in each module are unscored. College Board is testing them for future tests. You can't tell which ones they are, so treat every question as if it counts.
KADEN: Okay, scoring. What's a good score? Like, what's the number.
DEREK: Each section is scored from two hundred to eight hundred. Add them together and the total runs from four hundred to sixteen hundred.
DEREK: For context, the national average total for the class of twenty twenty-five was one thousand twenty-nine. That's from College Board's own report.
KADEN: So anything over that is good?
DEREK: Anything over that is above average. Whether it's good depends on where you're applying.
LEHUA: Right, and this is the part I want Big Island kids to hear. A good score is not one number. It's a number compared to the schools on your list.
DEREK: Most colleges publish a middle fifty percent range for their admitted or enrolled students. That means a quarter of those students scored below the low number, and a quarter scored above the high number. You can find it on the school's admissions page, or on College Board's BigFuture site.
DEREK: So the rule is this. If your score is inside that range, you're a normal applicant there. If it's at or above the top of the range, your score helps you. If it's below the bottom, think hard about whether to send it.
KADEN: What about UH? Most of my friends are going to UH.
DEREK: Good question. As of this fall, the flagship UH campus is test-optional. You choose whether to send a score. And they have what they call a "Do No Harm" policy. If a score you send would hurt your chances for admission or a scholarship, they leave it out.
KADEN: Wait, so there's no downside to sending it?
DEREK: For admission there, by their own policy, no. And some scholarships and some direct-entry programs may want a score, so a good score can still mean money. Check the admissions page for your year, because policies change.
LEHUA: What about mainland schools? Mainland public universities and private colleges.
DEREK: A lot of mainland public universities are test-optional too, and a strong score can still help with merit scholarships. Several highly selective private colleges have gone back to requiring scores in recent years. So the honest answer is, look up every school on your list, every year. Don't trust what your cousin heard two years ago.
PONO: Your cousin also said the North Shore was flat in December.
KADEN: My cousin lies a lot.
LEHUA: Okay, Derek, give him the one rule that changes how he takes the whole test.
DEREK: There is no guessing penalty. A wrong answer and a blank answer both earn zero points. So a blank can never help you. Answer every question.
KADEN: Every question? Even if I have no idea?
DEREK: Every question. We have a whole episode on making those guesses smarter by crossing out wrong answers. That's episode two.
LEHUA: Let's do a little tour of the actual test, because the tools are built in. Derek, Math first.
DEREK: In Math, about three quarters of the questions are multiple choice. The other quarter, you type in your own answer. That's called a student-produced response. And there's a Desmos graphing calculator built right into Bluebook. You can also bring an approved calculator of your own.
KADEN: Desmos is in there? That's kind of a cheat code.
DEREK: It's a tool, not a cheat code. Use it to graph and check, not to avoid learning the algebra. There's also a reference sheet with the main geometry formulas, and we'll go through what's on it in episode eleven.
LEHUA: And Reading and Writing?
PONO: Reading and Writing uses short passages. One short passage, one question. You are not reading a five-page story and answering ten questions about it. You read a paragraph, you answer one thing, and you move on.
KADEN: Okay, that's way less scary.
PONO: Way less. And every question has a flag to mark it for review, and a tool to cross out choices. And at the bottom there's a grid that shows every question and which ones you answered. That's your dashboard. Like the gauges on your truck.
KADEN: I don't have a truck. I have a bus pass.
PONO: Then it's like the bus schedule. You check it, you don't stare at it.
LEHUA: So let's recap the facts, then homework. Kaden, you do it.
KADEN: Okay. Digital, on Bluebook. Two sections, Reading and Writing, then Math. Two modules each. Twenty-seven questions in thirty-two minutes for Reading and Writing, twenty-two in thirty-five for Math. Module one decides module two, and the hard module two is good news. Scores from four hundred to sixteen hundred. No guessing penalty. Never leave a blank.
DEREK: That's a clean summary.
KADEN: Rate it.
DEREK: Eight.
KADEN: I'll take it.
LEHUA: Homework. Open the app. Take the placement check if you haven't. It's two questions per skill, and it tells the dashboard where to start you. Then tap the official practice button and look at Bluebook. You don't have to take a full test yet. Just open it, so it isn't a stranger on test day.
PONO: Know the place before you get there.
LEHUA: That's episode one. Episode two is crossing out, how to find the wrong answers. Thanks for listening, everybody.
KADEN: Can I finish my burrito now?
LEHUA: Finish your burrito.

check.q: How is the digital SAT structured?
choices: Two sections, Reading and Writing then Math, each split into two modules

check.q: If Module 2 feels harder than Module 1, what does that usually mean?
choices: You did well on Module 1 and unlocked the module that can score higher
Nothing, every Module 2 is the same

check.q: What is the rule about blank answers on the SAT?
choices: A blank costs a quarter point
A blank and a wrong answer both score zero, so answer every question
Blanks are fine in Math only
You can leave up to five blanks

sat.title: Crossing Out: How to Find the Wrong Answers
sat.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to SAT Notes, episode two. I'm Lehua. Sarah is here, Derek is here, and Kaden is here with a hoodie over his whole face.
KADEN: It's cold in here. I'm conserving heat.
SARAH: It's a recording booth, not a freezer.
LEHUA: Okay, Kaden, warm-up question from last time. What's the one rule about blanks on the SAT?
KADEN: No blanks. A wrong answer and a blank both get zero, so a blank can never help you. Answer everything.
DEREK: Correct. No guessing penalty.
LEHUA: Good. So if you have to answer everything, the next question is obvious. How do you answer well when you don't know? That's today. Crossing out.
SARAH: And I want to say this right away. Crossing out is not a backup plan for when you're lost. It's how good test takers find the right answer on purpose. You don't hunt for the right answer first. You hunt for the wrong ones, because wrong answers have fingerprints.
KADEN: Fingerprints?
SARAH: Patterns. The test writers build wrong answers on purpose, and they build them the same few ways every time. Once you know the patterns, you start seeing them everywhere.
DEREK: Let me do the math part first, because it's short. Every SAT multiple-choice question has four choices. A blind guess is one in four. Cross out one choice you can prove is wrong, and you're at one in three. Cross out two, and it's a coin flip. Cross out three, and you didn't guess at all. You solved it backward.
KADEN: Okay, that's actually kind of fire. Like a boss fight where you take out the minions first and the boss is just standing there alone.
LEHUA: There it is.
DEREK: And Bluebook has a tool for this built in. You can strike out choices right on the screen. The app has the same thing, a little x next to every choice.
SARAH: One rule with the x. Only cross out a choice when you can say why it's wrong. Out loud in your head, one sentence. If you can't say why, leave it standing.
KADEN: What happens if I cross out the right one by accident?
SARAH: The app will tell you. If you miss a question and you had crossed out the right answer, it says so. That's a sign you were tapping the x on a feeling, not a reason.
LEHUA: So, Sarah, the fingerprints. What are they?
SARAH: The app gives every wrong answer a name when you miss it. It shows up as a little label, like "Trap: opposite." There are ten names in the app. Today we'll use the six you meet most in Reading and Writing, because those are the ones you can spot while you read.
SARAH: One. Too extreme. The choice says always, never, completely, or proves, when the passage only says some or might.
SARAH: Two. Half right. The first half of the choice matches the passage, and the second half goes wrong.
SARAH: Three. True but irrelevant. The choice is a real detail from the passage, but it doesn't answer this question.
SARAH: Four. Opposite. The choice flips what the passage says. It uses the right topic, but points the wrong direction.
SARAH: Five. Adds an assumption. The choice needs one extra idea the passage never gave you.
SARAH: Six. Near miss. Mostly grammar. It looks almost right but has one small error, like a comma in the wrong place.
KADEN: That's a lot of names.
LEHUA: You don't have to memorize them today. When you miss one in the app, read the label. After a week, you'll know them the way you know your friends' ringtones.
SARAH: Let's do one. This is a Words in Context question. When I say "blank," that's the missing word. I'll read it twice. Kaden, just listen.
SARAH: "The coach was usually blunt, but after the loss she was unusually blank, choosing every word carefully so no player felt singled out." Which word fits the blank? A, blunt. B, diplomatic. C, timid. D, talkative.
SARAH: One more time. "The coach was usually blunt, but after the loss she was unusually blank, choosing every word carefully so no player felt singled out." A, blunt. B, diplomatic. C, timid. D, talkative.
LEHUA: Everybody listening, pause it and try. Cross out what you can, and say why.
LEHUA: Okay, we're back. Kaden, go.
KADEN: I want to say timid. Because she's being careful.
SARAH: Good, you're thinking, so let's walk it the slow way. Start with the clues. The sentence says usually blunt, but. That word "but" means the blank is going to be different from blunt. So which choice can we cross out first?
KADEN: A. Blunt. It's literally the word she's not being.
SARAH: Right. And that's the trap we're naming today. Opposite. The sentence flips away from blunt, and choice A flips it right back. Opposite answers love to borrow a word straight from the passage, because it feels familiar.
SARAH: Next clue. "Choosing every word carefully so no player felt singled out." That's about how she talks to people. Which choice has nothing to do with that?
KADEN: D. Talkative. Nothing says she talked a lot.
SARAH: Cross it out. Now it's timid against diplomatic. And this is where it gets good. Timid has the right idea. She is being careful. But timid means scared or shy. Does the sentence say she's scared?
KADEN: No. It says she's careful so nobody feels bad.
SARAH: So timid is right idea, wrong word. It's close in feeling but wrong in meaning. Diplomatic means careful with words so you don't hurt people. That matches every clue. The answer is B.
KADEN: Okay, so I was close.
DEREK: Close is how they get you. The test writers want you to stop at the first choice that feels okay.
SARAH: Here's the habit. Before you pick, cross out until you have a reason for every x. If you get down to two and they both feel fine, put each one into the sentence and read it again. The wrong one usually sounds off in one specific spot.
LEHUA: And what if you get down to two and still can't decide?
DEREK: Then you pick one and move on. You have a fifty-fifty shot, which is twice as good as a blind guess. Flag it if you want to come back. Don't burn two minutes on it.
LEHUA: My auntie posted "let's eat grandma" on her page last week. No comma. I screenshotted it for you, Sarah.
SARAH: I saw it. I commented with the comma. She did not ask.
KADEN: Did she reply?
SARAH: She deleted my comment. Worth it.
LEHUA: Okay, bring it home. Kaden, recap. In your own words.
KADEN: Okay. Don't hunt for the right answer first. Hunt for the wrong ones. Every cross-out makes a guess better, four to three to two. Only cross out when I can say why it's wrong. The app names the traps, like too extreme, half right, true but irrelevant, opposite, adds an assumption, and near miss. Today's trap was opposite, where the choice flips what the passage says, and it usually steals a word from the passage. And if I'm down to two, plug both in, pick one, and move on.
LEHUA: Derek?
DEREK: That was organized. You got all six names in order. Nine.
KADEN: Nine? What's a ten?
DEREK: Nobody knows.
LEHUA: Homework. Open the app and go to Drill. Pick Reading and Writing, the whole section. Use the x on every question, even the easy ones, and make yourself say why before you tap it. When you miss one, read the trap label. Get used to the names.
SARAH: And if you see "Trap: opposite," go back and find the word in the sentence that flipped it.
LEHUA: That's episode two. Next time is episode three, the time squeeze. Thanks for listening, everybody.
KADEN: Can I take the hoodie off now?
SARAH: You could have taken it off twenty minutes ago.

check.q: When should you tap the x to cross out an answer choice?
choices: Whenever a choice feels a little off
Only when you can say in one sentence why it is wrong
Only after you have picked your answer

check.q: "The coach was usually blunt, but after the loss she was unusually ___." Choice A is "blunt." Which trap is that?
You crossed out two choices and are down to two. What is your chance on a guess now?
choices: One in two, a coin flip

sat.title: The Time Squeeze
sat.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to SAT Notes, episode three. I'm Lehua. Today is the one everybody asks about. The clock. Coach Pono is here, Derek is here, and Kaden is here looking like he already ran out of time.
KADEN: I was up late. My alarm was early. It's a whole thing.
PONO: Kaden, that's the episode. You ran out of time before the test started. Welcome.
LEHUA: Warm-up from last time first. Kaden, when are you allowed to cross out a choice?
KADEN: Only when I can say why it's wrong. If I cross out the right one, the app calls me out.
LEHUA: Good. Hold on to that, it comes back today.
LEHUA: So, Coach, set it up. Why does the clock feel like it's attacking people?
PONO: Because they treat it like a bull. They fight it. You cannot fight a clock. The clock is a horse. You don't beat a horse, you ride it. You set a pace, you check it twice, and you don't let it decide where you're going.
DEREK: I'm going to say the actual numbers now, because Coach is going to keep saying horse.
PONO: I'm gonna keep saying horse.
DEREK: Reading and Writing. Two modules. Each one is twenty-seven questions in thirty-two minutes. That's about seventy-one seconds a question. Math. Two modules. Twenty-two questions in thirty-five minutes. About ninety-five seconds a question.
KADEN: Seventy-one seconds is nothing.
DEREK: Seventy-one seconds is plenty if you don't spend four minutes on question nine.
LEHUA: And that's the real problem, right? Nobody runs out of time evenly. They run out because of two or three questions that ate everything.
PONO: Exactly. The clock didn't beat you. One question beat you, and then the clock just told you about it.
KADEN: Okay so what do I actually do.
PONO: Two passes. First pass, you ride through in order. You look at a question. If you can see the path in about ten seconds, you take it. If you can't see the path, you pick your best guess, you flag it, and you move on. You do not sit there. Sitting there is fighting the horse.
KADEN: But what if I almost have it.
DEREK: "Almost have it" is the most expensive phrase on the SAT. Three more minutes on that one question is two or three questions you never reach. Those could be easy. The one you're stuck on, by definition, is not.
LEHUA: And when you guess, cross out first, like last episode.
DEREK: Right. Every choice you can prove wrong makes the guess better. One in four becomes one in three, then a coin flip. Small moves, real points.
LEHUA: Say the guessing rule, Derek, because people still don't believe it.
DEREK: There is no guessing penalty. None. On the SAT and on the ACT. A blank is a guaranteed zero. A guess at least has a chance. So a blank is the only answer that is always wrong.
KADEN: So I should just guess on everything?
DEREK: You should answer everything. Guessing is what you do when you've run out of better options. But the rule is, no blanks. Ever. Done.
PONO: Second pass. If you have time left, go back to the flags. You already have an answer on every one of them, so you're not rescuing anything, you're just upgrading. Start with the one that looked closest. Leave the monster for last. If the clock runs out while you're on the monster, who cares, you already answered it.
LEHUA: And on the digital SAT the flag is built in. There's a button. And there's a little grid at the bottom that shows you every question and whether you answered it. Use the grid. That's your dashboard.
KADEN: What about checkpoints? My tutor said something about checkpoints.
PONO: Your tutor's right. You look at the clock exactly twice. Not every thirty seconds. Twice. At the one-third mark and the two-thirds mark. And you ask one question. Am I at or past the target?
DEREK: Reading and Writing, that's question nine at ten minutes forty, and question eighteen at twenty-one minutes twenty. Math, question seven at eleven forty, and question fifteen at twenty-three twenty. Those are minutes used. The Bluebook clock counts down, so do that subtraction once before test day, not during it. The targets are in the app on the Time Squeeze page, you don't have to memorize them right now.
PONO: If you're behind, you flag faster. That's it. You don't panic, you don't speed-read, you just lower the bar for what you'll flag. If you're ahead, you slow down one notch.
KADEN: Being ahead is bad?
PONO: Ahead is fine. Ahead and careless is the problem. So use the extra time to read every word.
LEHUA: Let's talk about what happens in the last sixty seconds, because that's where people lose points they already had.
DEREK: In the last minute, you stop solving. Full stop. You open the grid, you look for anything unanswered, and you put something in. Then you stop. A half-finished solution is worth zero. A guess is worth something.
KADEN: What if I'm in the middle of a question and I have it?
DEREK: If you have it, you have it. Finish it, then check the grid. But "I have it" means you're writing the answer, not "I think I see where this goes."
LEHUA: Okay, Kaden, you're the one who actually takes this thing. What goes wrong for you?
KADEN: Honestly? Reading. I get into a passage and I read the whole thing like it's a book. Then the question is about one sentence and I'm like, I don't remember that sentence.
LEHUA: Yeah, that's the number one time leak in Reading and Writing. The digital SAT gives you one short passage per question. One. It's not a long passage with ten questions. So the move is, read the question first, then read the passage knowing what you're hunting for. That gets a whole episode of its own, episode five.
DEREK: Math version. Read the last sentence of the word problem first. That's the actual question. Then read the rest to collect the numbers. You'll stop doing arithmetic you didn't need.
KADEN: Okay that one's actually good.
LEHUA: One more thing, then the recap. The adaptive thing. The SAT is adaptive by module. Module one is a mix of easy, medium, and hard questions for everybody. Depending on how you do, module two is either the harder version or the easier version, and the harder version can score higher. So what does that mean for the clock?
DEREK: It means module one accuracy matters more than module one speed. Do not sprint module one to save time. There's no saving time, each module has its own clock. Get module one right, calmly, and you unlock the module that can give you the big score.
LEHUA: Kaden, recap. Your words.
KADEN: Two passes. First pass in order. If I can't see the path in about ten seconds, I guess, flag it, and go. Second pass, I upgrade the flags, closest one first, monster last. Check the clock twice, at one-third and two-thirds. Last minute, stop solving and fill the grid. Module one is about getting it right, not fast. And no blanks.
DEREK: That's the whole episode in one breath. Seven.
KADEN: Why not higher?
DEREK: You left out reading the question first.
LEHUA: Alright. Here's your homework. If you haven't done the placement check yet, do that first, it's two questions per skill and it tells the dashboard where to start you. Then go to Timed in the app. Do one Reading and Writing module, just one, with the checkpoints on. Don't worry about the score. Watch what the clock does to you. Then come back for episode four, Desmos.
KADEN: And flag stuff.
PONO: And flag stuff. No blanks.
DEREK: No blanks.
LEHUA: No blanks. That's episode three. Thanks for listening, everybody. Go catch your bus, Kaden.
KADEN: It left.
PONO: Should've flagged it.

check.q: Is there a guessing penalty on the SAT?
choices: Yes, a quarter point per wrong answer
No, a blank is the only answer that is always wrong

check.q: In the two-pass method, what do you do with a question you cannot see the path on in about ten seconds?
choices: Keep working until you get it
Leave it blank and move on
Pick your best guess, flag it, move on
Skip to the end of the module

check.q: How many times should you check the clock during a module?
choices: Twice, at the one-third and two-thirds marks

sat.title: Desmos Is Your Co-pilot
sat.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to SAT Notes, episode four. I'm Lehua. Derek is here, Coach Pono is here, and Kaden is here and he's already holding his phone like a calculator.
KADEN: I'm ready for math. Mentally.
PONO: Mentally is the hard part. Good start.
LEHUA: Callback first. Kaden, last episode was the time squeeze. Give me the plan in three pieces.
KADEN: Two passes. First pass, if I can't see the path in about ten seconds, I guess, flag it, and move on. Check the clock twice, at the one-third mark and the two-thirds mark. And no blanks.
PONO: That's it. Clean.
LEHUA: Okay. Today is Desmos. Derek, set it up.
DEREK: On the digital SAT, there's a Desmos graphing calculator built into Bluebook. It's there for the whole Math section, both modules. You can still bring your own approved calculator, but most students should learn the built-in one, because it's always there and it graphs.
KADEN: So it's like the game gives you a free power-up and most people never press the button.
DEREK: That's exactly it. And the power-up is this. If you can turn a question into equations, Desmos can draw them, and the answer is often a point you can tap.
LEHUA: Give me the big one.
DEREK: Systems of equations. Two lines. The question asks where they cross, or for the values that make both equations true. Same thing. Type the first equation on one line in Desmos, type the second on the next line, and look for where the lines meet. Tap that point. Desmos shows you the coordinates.
PONO: Okay, let's try one. Listen up, this one is short. I'll read it twice.
PONO: "The line y equals two x plus one and the line y equals negative x plus seven cross at the point x comma y. What is the value of y?" A, two. B, three. C, five. D, seven.
PONO: One more time. "The line y equals two x plus one and the line y equals negative x plus seven cross at the point x comma y. What is the value of y?" A, two. B, three. C, five. D, seven.
LEHUA: Pause it and try. Algebra or Desmos, your choice.
LEHUA: Okay, we're back. Kaden?
KADEN: I set them equal. Two x plus one equals negative x plus seven. Add x to both sides, three x plus one equals seven. Subtract one, three x equals six. x equals two. So A.
DEREK: Your algebra is perfect. Your answer is wrong.
KADEN: Bro. How.
DEREK: Read the last sentence of the question again. What did it ask for?
KADEN: The value of y. Oh no.
DEREK: Right. x is two. Now plug it back in. y equals two times two, plus one. That's five. The answer is C. And notice what they did. Two is sitting right there as choice A, waiting for you.
LEHUA: So that's the trap. Say the name.
DEREK: The app calls it answers the wrong part. You did real work, and you got a real number, but it's the answer to a question they didn't ask. With systems, the test loves to ask for y, or for x plus y, because they know a lot of students solve for x and stop.
PONO: Two habits fix it. Before you start, say out loud in your head what the question wants. Y. Then after you get a number, read the last sentence again before you tap anything.
DEREK: And here's how Desmos helps with this trap. Type both lines. Tap where they cross. Desmos shows two comma five. Both numbers are on the screen at the same time. Now you just pick the one they asked for.
KADEN: Okay, so Desmos is faster?
DEREK: For that one, about the same. Here's the honest part. Desmos is not always faster. Typing takes time. If the algebra is one or two steps, like three x plus four equals nineteen, just do it. You'll be done before you finish typing.
LEHUA: So when is Desmos the move?
DEREK: Three cases. One, systems where the numbers are messy, like fractions or decimals. Two, quadratics. If they ask for the solutions of x squared minus five x plus six equals zero, you can graph y equals that expression and tap where it crosses the x-axis. Those points, two and three, are the solutions. Three, checking. You solved it by hand, you have a little time left, so you graph it to confirm.
KADEN: What if the lines don't show up?
DEREK: Then zoom out. Sometimes the crossing is off the screen. If the lines look parallel, they might actually be parallel, which means no solution. That's a real answer choice sometimes.
PONO: Okay, here's how I think about it. Desmos is a good horse. A good horse knows the trail. But you still hold the reins. If you don't know where you're going, the horse just walks you in circles around the arena.
KADEN: Coach, every episode.
PONO: Every episode. And it's always true.
LEHUA: Derek, any typing tips? Because I've watched kids fight the keyboard for a minute on one equation.
DEREK: Three. Use parentheses more than you think you need. You don't need a times sign. Type two, then x, and Desmos reads it as two times x. And if a question uses letters other than x and y, rename them to x and y when you type, so it graphs like you expect.
LEHUA: And practice in the real thing.
DEREK: Yes. Open Bluebook before test day and play with the calculator. The free official practice is linked in the app under the official practice button. The first time you use Desmos should not be during the test.
LEHUA: The map app in my car works the same way. It's helpful, but only if I already know I'm going to Costco and not the other side of the island.
PONO: You going today?
LEHUA: It's Sunday. They close at six, and it's an hour away. I'm leaving right after this.
PONO: Then we go fast.
LEHUA: Kaden, recap for us. Your words.
KADEN: Okay. Desmos is built into Bluebook for all of Math. For a system, type both equations and tap where they cross, and that's your x and y. For a quadratic, graph it and tap where it hits the x-axis, those are the solutions. If the algebra is one or two steps, just do the algebra, because typing is slower. And the trap is answers the wrong part. I solved for x, but they wanted y. So say what they want before I start, and read the last sentence again before I pick.
DEREK: That's good. You even admitted the mistake in your own recap. Eight.

PONO: And keep using your checkpoints. Desmos doesn't stop the clock.

KADEN: Drive safe.

sat.title: Read the Question First
sat.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to SAT Notes, episode five. I'm Lehua. Sarah is here, Derek is here, and Kaden is here, and he made the bus today.
KADEN: I made the bus. I ran for it, but I made it. Driver waited like two seconds. Respect.
LEHUA: Okay, callback. Last episode was Desmos. Kaden, what was the trap, and what was the fix?
KADEN: Answers the wrong part. I solved for x and they wanted y. The fix is, say what the question wants before I start, and read the last sentence again before I pick.
DEREK: Good. That habit is going to show up again today, on the reading side.
LEHUA: Today is Reading and Writing. Sarah, it's yours.
SARAH: Today is one move. Predict, then match. It works on two kinds of questions. Words in Context, where there's a blank and you pick the word. And Central Ideas, where they ask what the passage is mostly saying.
SARAH: The move has three steps. First, read the question so you know what you're hunting for. Second, read the passage and make your own answer before you look at the choices. A word for a blank, or one short sentence for the main idea. Third, find the choice that matches your prediction.
KADEN: Why not just read the choices? They're right there.
SARAH: Because the choices are built to sound good. If you read them first, they plant ideas in your head. Four choices, and three of them were written to fool you. If you already have your own answer, you're comparing them to something solid instead of comparing them to each other.
DEREK: Same in math. You want your own number before you look at theirs.
LEHUA: Okay, let's try. Sarah, read it. No choices yet.
SARAH: Right. I'm going to read just the sentence twice. Your job is to come up with your own word for the blank. Here it is.
SARAH: "Researchers expected the new seedlings to struggle in the cold, but the plants proved surprisingly blank, surviving three frosts with little damage."
SARAH: Again. "Researchers expected the new seedlings to struggle in the cold, but the plants proved surprisingly blank, surviving three frosts with little damage."
LEHUA: Pause it and try. Say your own word out loud before we give you any choices.
LEHUA: And we're back. Kaden, your word?
KADEN: Tough.
SARAH: Tough is a great prediction. Where did you get it?
KADEN: It says they were supposed to struggle, but. So they didn't struggle. And they survived frosts.
SARAH: Exactly. Two clues. The word "but" flips the expectation, and "surviving three frosts" tells you which way it flipped. Now here are the choices. A, fragile. B, resilient. C, indestructible. D, colorful.
SARAH: Once more. A, fragile. B, resilient. C, indestructible. D, colorful.
KADEN: Okay. Fragile is out, that's the opposite of tough. Colorful is random. So it's resilient or indestructible.
SARAH: And which one matches "tough" better?
KADEN: Honestly indestructible sounds tougher.
SARAH: And that's the trap. Listen to the last part of the sentence again. "With little damage." Little damage is still some damage. Indestructible means nothing can hurt it at all. That's more than the sentence says.
DEREK: That's the app's trap name. Too extreme.
SARAH: Too extreme. The choice goes past what the text supports. It's the right direction, but it goes too far. Resilient means able to recover or hold up under stress. That matches tough, and it matches little damage. Plug it back in. "The plants proved surprisingly resilient, surviving three frosts with little damage." Reads right. The answer is B.
KADEN: So the trap was basically my own prediction, but louder.
SARAH: That's a perfect way to say it. Too extreme choices are the loud version of the right answer. Listen for words like always, never, completely, impossible, proves. Then go back and check whether the passage was really that strong.
LEHUA: Now the Central Ideas version. Same move, different target.
SARAH: For Central Ideas, you read the whole short passage, then say the main point in one short sentence, before the choices. Then you match. Two extra things to watch. A choice can be too narrow, which means it's about one detail, not the whole passage. Or it can be too broad, which means it covers more than this passage actually says.
SARAH: And too extreme shows up here a lot. The passage says a study suggests something, and the choice says the study proves it. Suggests and proves are not the same strength.
DEREK: In math terms, the passage said "probably." The choice said "always." That's a different number.
LEHUA: What about time? Kaden's going to ask.
KADEN: I was going to ask.
SARAH: The prediction takes about five seconds once you practice. It saves time, because you stop reading every choice three times. When you have your own word, two choices fall away right away.
LEHUA: And if you can't predict anything?
SARAH: Then predict the direction. Positive or negative. Strong or weak. Even that crosses out a choice or two. Then use what we did in episode two. Cross out with a reason.
KADEN: Okay, real question. Sarah, do you predict when you read texts from people?
SARAH: I predict where the commas should be. That's different. My mom texted the family chat, "Pick up milk eggs and rice." No commas. I asked her what a milk egg is.
LEHUA: Did she answer?
SARAH: She sent the list again. Same list. Still no commas.
LEHUA: Recap time. Kaden, go.
KADEN: Read the question first so I know what I'm hunting. Then read the passage and make my own answer before I look. One word for a blank, one short sentence for a main idea. Then match. The trap is too extreme. It's the right direction but louder than the passage, like indestructible when the passage said little damage. Watch for always, never, proves. And for main ideas, not too narrow, not too broad.
DEREK: That was solid. The "my prediction but louder" line was good. Eight.
KADEN: I keep getting eight.
DEREK: You keep earning eight.
LEHUA: Homework. In the app, go to Drill and pick Words in Context. Do ten. On every one, cover the choices with your hand, or just look away from the screen, and say your word out loud before you look. When you miss one and it says "Trap: too extreme," go back and find the part of the passage that was softer than the choice.
SARAH: And open the Strategies tab for Words in Context. The steps are right there.
LEHUA: That's episode five. Next time, episode six, is the smallest step, inferences and evidence. Thanks for listening, everybody.
SARAH: Kaden, prediction for your rating next episode?
KADEN: Eight.
DEREK: Don't predict my ratings.

act.title: How the ACT Works
act.transcript:
LEHUA: Welcome to ACT Notes, episode one. I'm Lehua. Same crew, different test. Sarah is here, Derek is here, Coach Pono is here, and Kaden is here early for once.
KADEN: The bus was early. I did not plan this.
PONO: New show, new hat.
SARAH: It's the same hat, Coach.
PONO: It's a different hat.
LEHUA: Okay. Kaden, what do you know about the ACT right now?
KADEN: It's the other one. The one with science. And it's faster? That's what my friend said.
DEREK: Your friend is right on both counts, with one update. Let me lay it out, because the test changed in twenty twenty-five, and a lot of what's online is out of date.
DEREK: The ACT has three required sections. English, Math, and Reading, in that order. Science used to be required. Now it is optional. You pick whether to add it when you register.
KADEN: Wait, so no science?
DEREK: Only if you want it. We'll get to who should want it.
SARAH: Here are the numbers. English is fifty questions in thirty-five minutes. Math is forty-five questions in fifty minutes. Reading is thirty-six questions in forty minutes.
SARAH: Add Science and that's forty more questions in forty minutes. The core test without Science is about two hours and five minutes of actual testing.
KADEN: That's shorter than the old one?
SARAH: Shorter, and fewer questions. Which means each question counts a little more. Keep that in your head.
LEHUA: Coach, pace. Everybody says the ACT is fast. Is it?
PONO: It's faster than the SAT per question, yes. Listen, dis one you gotta hear.
PONO: English gives you about forty-two seconds a question. Math gives you about sixty-seven. Reading, about sixty-seven. Science, about sixty.
KADEN: Forty-two seconds? For English?
PONO: Forty-two seconds for a question you can answer in fifteen if you know the rule. English questions are short. The clock is not the enemy. Reading the whole passage three times is the enemy.
PONO: The clock is a horse. You ride it, you don't fight it. We'll spend a whole episode on pace. Episode three.
LEHUA: Scoring. Derek, what's the number everybody talks about?
DEREK: Each section gets a score from one to thirty-six. The number people talk about is the Composite. It's the average of English, Math, and Reading, rounded to the nearest whole number. Also one to thirty-six.
KADEN: So a thirty-six is perfect.
DEREK: A thirty-six is perfect, and almost nobody gets it, and you don't need it. For context, the national average Composite for the class of twenty twenty-five was nineteen point four. That's from ACT's own report. Whether your score is good depends on where you're applying.
LEHUA: And a good score is not one number, right? Same thing we said on the SAT show.
DEREK: Same thing. Most colleges publish a middle fifty percent range for the students they admit or enroll. If your Composite sits inside that range, you're a normal applicant there. At or above the top of the range, the score helps you. Below the bottom, think about whether to send it.
SARAH: And a lot of schools, including UH's flagship campus, are test-optional. That means you choose whether to send a score. A good one can still mean scholarship money, so don't skip the test just because a school says optional.
LEHUA: And Science?
DEREK: Science gets its own score, one to thirty-six, reported next to the Composite, not inside it. If you take Science, you also get a STEM score, which averages your Math and Science.
KADEN: So should I take Science or not?
SARAH: Take it if you're applying to engineering, nursing, pre-med, anything with a science major, or to any school that says it wants it. Some schools and some scholarships still look for it. When in doubt, take it. A school that doesn't use it can just ignore it.
DEREK: And the Science section isn't biology trivia. It's reading charts and tables. We have a whole episode on it, episode eleven. The app has a toggle in Settings if you want the Science drills.
LEHUA: Guessing rule. Say it.
DEREK: There is no guessing penalty. A blank and a wrong answer both score zero. So a blank is the only answer that is always wrong. Answer every question.
KADEN: Same as the SAT.
DEREK: Same as the SAT. Points for remembering.
KADEN: How many points?
DEREK: Save it for the recap.
LEHUA: Now the practical stuff. Where do you sign up?
SARAH: You make a free MyACT account at act dot org. That's where you register, pick a test date and a test center, choose Science or Writing, and later see your scores. Writing is an essay, forty minutes, also optional. Most schools don't need it. Check your list.
SARAH: The test runs about seventy dollars this year, a little more if you add Science or the essay. Check act dot org for the current price. If that's a problem, go to your counselor. There are fee waivers, and they also cover sending scores.
KADEN: Online or paper?
SARAH: Both exist. You pick at registration based on what your test center offers. Same sections, same scoring. If you take it online, the timer is on screen. If you take it on paper, bring sharpened number two pencils, not mechanical ones, and a watch with no alarm.
LEHUA: Superscore. People hear that word and get confused.
DEREK: Superscore means if you take the ACT more than once, ACT will combine your best English, best Math, and best Reading from different dates into one Composite. Many colleges accept it. Some only look at your best single date. So taking it twice is usually smart. Three times, fine. Six times, you're studying wrong.
KADEN: Okay, so SAT or ACT. Which one do I take?
LEHUA: That's episode two, the whole thing. Short version, take one practice test of each and see which one feels like your brain. Any college that looks at scores takes either one.
PONO: Including the university in Hilo. Both tests, no favorites.
PONO: Let's recap. Kaden, you do it.
KADEN: Three required sections. English, Math, Reading. Science optional, and I should probably take it. Scores one to thirty-six. Composite is the average of the three. No guessing penalty, no blanks. Sign up on MyACT. Fee waivers through the counselor. Superscore means best sections across dates.
DEREK: Clean. Seven. Some of that was my line.
KADEN: I'll take it.
LEHUA: Homework. Open the app, flip the toggle to ACT, and take the placement check if you haven't. It's two questions per skill and it tells the dashboard where to start you. Then tap the official practice button and look at the free practice on act dot org. Don't take it yet. Just look.
LEHUA: That's episode one. Episode two is SAT versus ACT, which one fits you. Thanks for listening, and I have to get to Costco before it closes.
KADEN: It's Saturday.
LEHUA: Seven o'clock. I know. That's why I'm leaving now.

act.title: SAT or ACT?
act.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to ACT Notes, episode two. I'm Lehua. Sarah is here, Derek is here, and Kaden is here holding two breakfast sandwiches.
KADEN: One is for later.
SARAH: It's nine in the morning.
KADEN: Later is ten.
LEHUA: Okay. Warm-up from last time. Kaden, what's the Composite?
KADEN: The average of English, Math, and Reading, rounded to a whole number. Science doesn't count in it.
DEREK: Correct. Science is reported next to it, not inside it.
LEHUA: Good. Today is the question every junior asks. SAT or ACT? And the answer is not a vibe. It's a test. Actually two tests.
SARAH: Here's the whole plan in one sentence. Take one official practice test of each, timed, and see which one fits your brain. Both are free. The official practice links in the app take you to each one. Flip the test toggle to see the other side.
KADEN: Two whole practice tests? That's like four hours.
SARAH: Somewhere around four to five hours, on two different days. Compared to the months you'll spend studying for the wrong test, it's cheap.
LEHUA: And colleges don't care which one, right?
DEREK: Any college that looks at scores takes either one. So the only question is which test you'll score better on. There are four big differences. Let's go through them.
DEREK: Difference one. Pace. The ACT gives you less time per question. English is about forty-two seconds a question. Math and Reading are about sixty-seven. On the SAT, Reading and Writing is about seventy-one seconds a question, and Math is about ninety-five.
KADEN: That's a big gap.
DEREK: It is. So let's feel it. Here's a quick one for you and for everybody listening. ACT Math is forty-five questions in fifty minutes. About how many seconds is that per question?
DEREK: One more time. Forty-five questions, fifty minutes. Seconds per question?
LEHUA: Pause it and try. No calculator, just round.
LEHUA: Okay, we're back. Kaden?
KADEN: Fifty minutes is, um, three thousand seconds. Three thousand divided by forty-five. Forty-five times sixty is twenty-seven hundred, so it's a little more than sixty. Sixty-something.
DEREK: Good. Three thousand divided by forty-five is about sixty-six point seven. Call it sixty-seven seconds. The SAT gives you about ninety-five on math. That's almost half a minute more on every single question.
DEREK: And here's the classic way to miss that one. You do fifty divided by forty-five, get about one point one, and stop. That's minutes, and the question asked for seconds. The app calls that trap answers the wrong part. Read what the question asks for before you pick.
KADEN: So if I'm slow, SAT.
DEREK: If you're accurate but slow, the SAT might fit better. If you're quick and you don't mind a fast clock, the ACT might. That's exactly what the practice tests will show you. Where did you run out of time, and how much did you leave unfinished?
LEHUA: Difference two. Calculators.
DEREK: Both tests let you use a calculator on every math question. The SAT has a graphing calculator built right into Bluebook. On the ACT, you can use an approved calculator for the whole math section. If you take the ACT online, there's a graphing calculator built into the screen too, and you can still bring your own. Check the calculator policy on act dot org before test day so you don't show up with the wrong one.
DEREK: The other math difference is the formula sheet. The SAT gives you a reference sheet with the main formulas. The ACT does not. You memorize them. We have a whole episode on the short list, episode nine.
LEHUA: Difference three. Science.
SARAH: The ACT has an optional Science section. Forty questions in forty minutes. The SAT has no Science section at all. And ACT Science is mostly reading charts and tables fast. If charts are your thing, that's a point for the ACT. If you want to skip it, you can, but think about the schools you're applying to first.
KADEN: I like charts. Charts don't have feelings.
SARAH: Charts have units, which is worse.
LEHUA: Difference four. Reading style. Sarah, this is yours.
SARAH: On the SAT, every Reading and Writing question has its own short passage. One passage, one question, done. On the ACT, Reading is four longer passages, and each one has several questions. So on the ACT, you're holding a whole passage in your head while you answer a bunch of questions about it.
KADEN: So the SAT is like short videos and the ACT is like a full episode.
SARAH: That's annoyingly accurate. Some people like the short ones because they reset every question. Some people like the long ones because once you understand the passage, the questions go faster. You won't know which one you are until you try both.
LEHUA: Okay, so what do I actually compare after the two practice tests? Don't just compare scores, right?
SARAH: Right. The two tests use different scales, so comparing a number on one to a number on the other is not as simple as it looks. Compare three things instead. One, where did you finish? Did you get to the end of each section, or did the clock beat you? Two, which sections felt like you were guessing? Three, which test did you want to keep going on?
DEREK: And be honest about number three. You're about to spend months with this test. Pick the one you can stand.
KADEN: Like picking a main in a fighting game. You gotta like playing them or you quit.
LEHUA: There it is.
LEHUA: One more question people always ask. Should I just study for both?
DEREK: Not at the start. Pick one, get good at it, and take it. The skills overlap a lot. Grammar is grammar, algebra is algebra. But pacing and format are different, and splitting your practice between two formats slows you down on both.
SARAH: And whichever one you pick, the rule from episode one still holds. No blanks. No guessing penalty on either test.
LEHUA: Kaden, recap. Your words.
KADEN: Take one free official practice test of each, timed. The four differences are pace, calculator and formulas, Science, and reading style. ACT is faster, about sixty-seven seconds a math question instead of ninety-five. Both let you use a calculator, but only the SAT gives you a formula sheet. ACT has optional Science, SAT has none. SAT is one short passage per question, ACT is four long ones. Then compare where I finished, where I guessed, and which one I can stand. Pick one.
DEREK: You did the arithmetic in your head and remembered it. Eight.
KADEN: Eight! I'll take an eight.
LEHUA: Homework. Open the app, go to Timed, and do one ACT section. Just one. English is the shortest at thirty-five minutes. See how the clock feels. Then tap the official practice button and plan a day for the full free practice test on each side.
LEHUA: That's episode two. Next time is episode three, Forty-Two Seconds, all about pace. Thanks for listening. I gotta go. I promised myself one hour at the record store in town before dinner.
KADEN: One hour?
LEHUA: One hour is a pace. Two hours is a problem.

act.title: Forty-Two Seconds
act.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to ACT Notes, episode three. I'm Lehua. Coach Pono is here, Derek is here, and Kaden is here, technically.
KADEN: I'm here. My eyes are still loading.
PONO: Good. Today's about the clock. You'll wake up.
LEHUA: Warm-up from last time. Kaden, name one of the four differences between the SAT and the ACT.
KADEN: Pace. The ACT gives you less time per question. Like sixty-seven seconds on math instead of ninety-five.
LEHUA: Good. And that's today. The ACT is fast. So how do you not drown?
DEREK: Numbers first, then Coach can do the fun part. English, forty-two seconds a question. Math, sixty-seven. Reading, sixty-seven. Science, if you take it, sixty.
KADEN: Forty-two seconds still sounds fake.
PONO: Forty-two is plenty for most English questions. Most of them are short. One underlined part, four choices. If you know the rule, you're done in fifteen seconds. The trouble is never the easy ones. The trouble is the one question you sit on for three minutes.
LEHUA: Because nobody runs out of time evenly.
PONO: Right. Two or three questions eat the clock, and then the clock tells you about it at the end. So here's the plan. Two passes. Listen, dis part important.
PONO: First pass, go in order. Look at the question. If you can see the path in about ten seconds, do it. If you can't, pick your best guess, mark it, and move on. Online, use the flag. On paper, circle the question number in your test booklet. Don't sit there.
PONO: Second pass, with whatever time is left, go back to the ones you marked. Easiest-looking first, the monster last. You already put a guess on every one, so you're just upgrading.
DEREK: And the last sixty seconds, you stop solving. Check that every question has an answer. No blanks. There's no guessing penalty, so a blank is the only answer that's always wrong.
PONO: It's like barrel racing. You go around the barrel, you don't stop to look at it. The one you knocked over, you deal with later.
KADEN: I don't know anything about barrel racing.
PONO: You know enough now.
LEHUA: Okay, checkpoints. Coach, how often should you look at the clock?
PONO: Twice. Not every minute. Twice. At one-third of the time and two-thirds of the time. And you ask one question. Am I at or past the target question?
DEREK: The targets. English, question seventeen at eleven minutes forty, and question thirty-three at twenty-three twenty. Math, question fifteen at sixteen minutes forty, and question thirty at thirty-three twenty. Reading is passages, not questions. Four passages, about ten minutes each, so passage two should be done at twenty minutes.
KADEN: I'm not memorizing all that.
DEREK: You don't have to today. They're on the Time Squeeze page in the app. But here's a nice thing. Those times are minutes used. If you test online, the timer on screen counts down. And for English and Math, the checkpoints are mirror images. In English, eleven forty used means twenty-three twenty left. Twenty-three twenty used means eleven forty left. Same two numbers, flipped.
KADEN: Wait, that's actually clean.
DEREK: Math too. Sixteen forty and thirty-three twenty, both ways.
LEHUA: Let's try one. Kaden, and everybody listening. You're in English. The clock says you've used eleven minutes and forty seconds. You just finished question fourteen. Are you on pace, and what do you do?
LEHUA: Again. English. Eleven forty used. You just finished question fourteen. On pace or not, and what do you do?
PONO: Pause it and try.
PONO: Okay. Kaden.
KADEN: The target at eleven forty is seventeen. I'm on fourteen. So I'm behind by three.
PONO: Behind by three. That's only half of it. The question also asked what you do. Stop at "behind" and the app would call that stopped a step early. So, now what? This is where people panic.
KADEN: Go faster?
PONO: No. Don't read faster. Reading faster makes mistakes. You flag faster. You lower the bar. If a question doesn't show you the path in ten seconds, it gets a guess and a mark, right now, no thinking about it. That's how you catch up. You stop feeding the slow ones.
DEREK: Three questions behind at forty-two seconds each is about two minutes. Flag the next slow one at ten seconds instead of fighting it for two minutes, and you've made most of that back.
KADEN: And if I'm ahead?
PONO: Slow down one notch. Ahead is fine. Ahead and careless is the problem. Use the extra seconds to read every word of the question.
LEHUA: The app does this for you, right?
DEREK: In Timed, it checks you at one-third and two-thirds. It'll say on pace, or it'll say behind pace, flag the long ones and move. Same words Coach just said.
PONO: The app stole my line.
DEREK: You stole it first.
KADEN: Okay, what about Reading? That's where I die.
PONO: Reading is ten minutes a passage. No exceptions. If a passage is eating you alive at minute nine, you answer what's left with your best guesses and you go to the next passage. The next passage might be your best one. Don't let a bad one steal the time from a good one.
KADEN: That's like my cousin's car. The gas light comes on and he says it's fine for another twenty miles. It's never fine.
LEHUA: So the gas light is your checkpoint.
KADEN: The gas light is my checkpoint. Okay, I get it.
LEHUA: Last thing. If you test on paper, there's no clock on your screen. So what do you bring?
DEREK: A watch with no alarm. And practice with that same watch, so you're not figuring it out on test day.
LEHUA: Kaden, recap. Your words.
KADEN: Forty-two seconds for English, sixty-seven for Math and Reading, sixty for Science. Two passes. First pass in order, ten seconds to see the path or guess, mark it, move. Second pass, go back easiest first. Last minute, no blanks. Check the clock twice, one-third and two-thirds. English is seventeen at eleven forty, and the countdown shows the same numbers flipped. Behind means flag faster, not read faster. Reading is ten minutes a passage.
DEREK: You got the mirror trick. That was the best part. Seven.
KADEN: Only seven?
DEREK: You skipped the Math targets. They were mirrors too.
LEHUA: Homework. Open the app, go to Timed, and do one ACT section with checkpoints on. English is a good start. When the checkpoint pops up, notice how you feel, not just the number. Then come back for episode four, punctuation.
LEHUA: That's episode three. Thanks for listening. I'm out, I have cycling practice with a friend who's training for the Ironman.
KADEN: Are you doing the Ironman?
LEHUA: No. I'm doing the part where I try to keep up for one hour.
PONO: Same as the test. Pace.

act.title: Where the Sentence Breaks, ACT Edition
act.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to ACT Notes, episode four. I'm Lehua. Sarah is here, Derek is here, and Kaden is here, and I think his eyes finished loading.
KADEN: Ninety percent. Still buffering a little.
SARAH: That's progress.
LEHUA: Warm-up from last time. Kaden, ACT English. What question should you be on at eleven minutes forty?
KADEN: Seventeen. And if I'm behind, I flag faster, not read faster.
LEHUA: Good. So how do you get through English questions fast enough to make seventeen? You know the rules cold. Today is a rule that shows up all over the English section. Where the sentence breaks. Sarah, you've been waiting all week.
SARAH: I have. My mom texted me this morning. "I'm at the store, I'll be home soon."
KADEN: That's a normal text.
SARAH: It's a comma splice. Two complete sentences glued together with only a comma. I texted back a semicolon.
LEHUA: Just the semicolon?
SARAH: Just the semicolon. She knows what it means.
DEREK: Does she?
SARAH: She does now.
LEHUA: Okay, teach it. Why does punctuation matter so much on ACT English?
SARAH: Because punctuation questions show up again and again, and they're some of the most learnable points on the whole test. There are only a few rules. Once you know them, these questions take you ten seconds.
SARAH: Here's the move. The app calls it "what's on each side." Find the punctuation mark being tested. Then look left of it and right of it, and label each side. Is it a full sentence that could stand alone? Or is it just a piece, a phrase?
KADEN: How do I know if it's a full sentence?
SARAH: It has a subject and a verb, and it makes sense if you put a period after it. "The tide was low." Full sentence. "When the tide was low." Not a full sentence. That word "when" makes it wait for something.
SARAH: Now the rule. If both sides are full sentences, you have three options. A period. A semicolon. Or a comma plus a joining word like and, but, or so. That's it. A comma by itself is not allowed. That's the comma splice my mom did.
DEREK: So a semicolon is basically a period that doesn't end the sentence.
SARAH: Between two full sentences, yes. Exactly that.
SARAH: And two more marks. A colon and a dash. On the ACT, the safe rule is that the part before a colon has to be a full sentence. The colon says, here comes the thing I promised. Same for a dash when it's setting something up.
KADEN: Like a semicolon is a save point. The level ends, but you keep going.
SARAH: I will allow that.
LEHUA: Okay. Let's do one. Sarah, read it.
SARAH: I'll read the sentence, then the four choices. Listen for where the sentence breaks. "The tide was low, we walked out to the reef." The underlined part is "low, we." Choices. A, No Change, so low comma we. B, low semicolon we. C, low we, with no punctuation at all. D, low semicolon and we.
SARAH: One more time. "The tide was low, we walked out to the reef." A, low comma we. B, low semicolon we. C, low we, nothing. D, low semicolon and we.
LEHUA: Pause it and try. Label each side first.
LEHUA: Okay, we're back. Kaden.
KADEN: Left side, "The tide was low." That's a full sentence. Right side, "we walked out to the reef." Also full. So both sides are full sentences.
SARAH: Good. That's the whole question right there. Now which choices are allowed for two full sentences?
KADEN: Period, semicolon, or comma plus and. So B, the semicolon.
SARAH: B. Let's kill the others, because the wrong ones are the lesson. C has nothing between two full sentences. That's a run-on. Cross it out. D has a semicolon and the word and together. You use one or the other, not both. Cross it out.
SARAH: And A. A is the trap we're naming today. The app calls it near miss. It looks almost right. It's one tiny mark away from correct. If it said comma and, it would be fine. With just the comma, it's a comma splice. And it's the one people pick because it sounds right when you say it out loud.
KADEN: Because you pause there.
SARAH: Because you pause there. That's the other trap the app warns you about: adding commas wherever you would pause when you're talking. Your voice is not a punctuation rule. Label the sides instead.
DEREK: Also, notice that A was No Change. On the ACT, No Change is right sometimes. Not always, not never. Don't avoid it, and don't fall in love with it. Test it like any other choice.
LEHUA: Okay, Sarah, one more piece. Apostrophes, quick.
SARAH: Quick. Ask two questions. Does something own something? And how many owners? One student's notebook, apostrophe before the s. Two students' notebooks, apostrophe after the s. And "its" with no apostrophe means belonging to it. "It's" with an apostrophe means it is. Say "it is" in the sentence. If that works, use the apostrophe.
KADEN: That's the one I always mess up.
SARAH: Everybody does. That's why it's on the test.
LEHUA: And in the app, when you miss one of these, you'll see that label. Trap, near miss. So you'll know it was almost right, and you can find the one tiny mark that broke it.
DEREK: Then it goes in your error log, and you redo it in three days.
LEHUA: Kaden, recap. Your words.
KADEN: Find the mark, then label both sides. Full sentence or just a piece. Two full sentences get a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus and, but, or so. Comma alone is a comma splice. A colon needs a full sentence before it. No Change is sometimes right, so test it. The trap was near miss, like the comma that's one word away from right. Don't put commas where you pause. Its with no apostrophe means belonging to it.
DEREK: That was every rule, in order, with the trap. Eight.
KADEN: Eight. Up from last week.
DEREK: Don't get comfortable.
LEHUA: Homework. Open the app, go to Drill, and pick the punctuation skill. Before every answer, say both labels in your head, full or piece, then pick the mark. When you miss one, read the trap label.
LEHUA: That's episode four. Next time is episode five, Shorter Is Usually Right. Thanks for listening, everybody. I gotta run. Somebody told me there's one slice of chocolate cake left at the barbecue place on the main road.
KADEN: Who told you that?
LEHUA: Nobody. But if I leave now, it's true.

check.q: "The tide was low, we walked out to the reef." Which fix is correct?
Choice A, "low, we," is one small mark away from correct. Which trap is that?
What does the app say to do before you pick a punctuation mark?
choices: Put a comma wherever you would pause
Label each side: full sentence or just a piece

act.title: Shorter Is Usually Right
act.transcript:
LEHUA: Hey, welcome back to ACT Notes, episode five. I'm Lehua. Sarah is here, Derek is here, and Kaden is here and already eating.
KADEN: It's a musubi. It's brain food.
SARAH: It's rice food.
LEHUA: Warm-up from last time. Kaden, two full sentences. What can you put between them?
KADEN: A period, a semicolon, or a comma plus and, but, or so. Comma alone is a comma splice.
SARAH: Perfect.
LEHUA: Good. Today is the rest of grammar. Sarah, the title of this episode is "Shorter Is Usually Right." Is that true?
SARAH: Usually. On ACT English, when two choices say the same thing and both are correct, the shorter one tends to win. Extra words that repeat an idea are wrong on this test. But notice the word usually. Shorter loses when it breaks a rule. So today is two rules, and then the shortcut.
SARAH: Rule one. Strip to the core. Find the subject and the verb, and cross out everything between them. Listen. "The box of old records are on the shelf." Sounds kind of okay, right?
KADEN: Kind of.
SARAH: Cross out "of old records." Now it's "The box are on the shelf."
KADEN: Oh, that's bad. The box is.
SARAH: The box is. The verb matches the box, not the records. The app warns you about this exact trap: matching the verb to a nearby noun instead of the real subject. The test often puts a plural noun right next to the verb to pull you in.
SARAH: Same idea for pronouns. A pronoun has to match the noun it stands for in number. "The team lost its first game." The team is one team, so on the ACT it's its, not their.
SARAH: And tense. Keep the verbs in the same time as the rest of the passage. If the paragraph is in the past, a random present-tense verb is probably the wrong answer.
LEHUA: Rule two. Modifiers.
SARAH: A modifier is a describing phrase. The rule is that it has to sit right next to the thing it describes. When that thing is in the wrong spot, it's a misplaced modifier. When it's missing from the sentence completely, it's a dangling modifier. Either way, the sentence says something ridiculous.
LEHUA: Let's do one. Read it twice.
SARAH: "Driving up the hill, the fog made the road hard to see." Which version is correct? A, No Change. B, "Driving up the hill, we could barely see the road through the fog." C, "While driving up the hill, the fog made the road hard to see." D, "Driving up the hill, the road was hard to see in the fog."
SARAH: Again. "Driving up the hill, the fog made the road hard to see." A, No Change. B, "Driving up the hill, we could barely see the road through the fog." C, "While driving up the hill, the fog made the road hard to see." D, "Driving up the hill, the road was hard to see in the fog."
LEHUA: Pause it and try. Ask who's driving.
LEHUA: Okay, we're back. Kaden, who's driving?
KADEN: In A, the fog. The fog is driving up the hill. Which, okay, that's kind of how it feels in my uncle's truck, but no.
SARAH: Right. The phrase "driving up the hill" attaches to whatever comes right after the comma. In A, that's the fog. Cross it out. D?
KADEN: D, the road is driving. Also no.
SARAH: Cross it out. Now C. C is the trap we're naming today. Near miss. It changed one thing. It added "while." It looks like somebody fixed it. But the next word is still "the fog," so the fog is still driving. One small change, still broken.
KADEN: So B. "We" are driving.
SARAH: B. The people are right after the comma, so the people are driving. And here's the twist. B is the longest choice.
KADEN: So the title is lying.
SARAH: The title says usually. Shorter wins only among the choices that are correct. Grammar first, then length. Rule, then shortcut.
DEREK: That's the same as math. The shortcut only counts if the answer is right.
LEHUA: Okay, now the shortcut itself.
SARAH: Redundancy. Saying the same thing twice. "In my opinion, I think the plan is good." "In my opinion" and "I think" are the same idea. Cut one. "The hotel was built recently, a few months ago." Recently and a few months ago, same idea. Cut one.
SARAH: And sometimes one of the choices is OMIT. That means delete the underlined part completely. When the sentence still makes sense and keeps its meaning without those words, OMIT is often right. So the habit is to check OMIT or the shortest choice first. If it keeps the meaning and it's grammatical, take it.
KADEN: So OMIT is like the skip button.
SARAH: OMIT is the skip button, but only when you lose nothing by skipping.
DEREK: And don't pick it because it's short. Read the sentence without the words. If it still says the same thing, good. If the meaning changes, it's wrong.
LEHUA: Sarah, how fast should these go?
SARAH: Fast. Grammar questions are where you bank time for the harder ones. Strip to the core, check the modifier, check the shortest. That's maybe fifteen seconds when you know the rules. That buys you time for the questions about what a paragraph is trying to do. That's next week.
LEHUA: And in the app, when you miss one, you'll see the label "Trap, near miss." That's your hint that the choice you picked fixed something, just not the real problem.
DEREK: Then find the one word that broke it, and redo the question when the error log says it's due. That's what the redo in three days is for.
LEHUA: Kaden, recap. Your words.
KADEN: Two rules and a shortcut. One, strip to the core. Cross out the stuff between the subject and the verb, then match them. Same with pronouns, and keep the tense the same. Two, the describing phrase has to sit next to what it describes, so ask who's doing it. Then the shortcut. Don't say the same thing twice. Check OMIT or the shortest choice first, but only if it's still correct. Grammar first, then shorter. The trap was near miss, like adding "while" and the fog is still driving.
DEREK: The fog is still driving. You'll remember that. Eight.
KADEN: The fog is still driving. That's going on a shirt.
LEHUA: Homework. Open the app, go to Drill, and pick grammar and usage. On every question, do the strip. Cross out the middle in your head and match the subject and verb. Then check the Strategies tab for the four steps if you get stuck.
LEHUA: That's episode five. Next time is episode six, What Is This Sentence For. Thanks for listening, everybody. I'm going to bed early. Saturday morning hike up to the pond.
KADEN: How early?
LEHUA: Early enough that the fog is still driving.
